rule: Deterministic script → language. Only a script that pins a language unambiguously gets an answer; everything else defers to the model.
why: Both ends bucket a translation by source language. When they disagree, the same word lands in different buckets on phone and desktop — the museum's by-language lens and the concept clustering split apart. The mixed-script cases below are where they used to disagree.
note: `expected: null` means the script doesn't settle it (bare Han is ambiguous between Chinese and kanji-only Japanese; Latin spans dozens of languages) and the model's own report fills it in. Consumed by core/tests/test_source_language.py; the Android JUnit suite still carries its own copy — wiring it to read this file needs a Gradle sourceSets change and a device run.

cases.note: bare Han is genuinely ambiguous — Chinese or kanji-only Japanese
Latin is shared across dozens of languages
Latin with diacritics is still Latin
THE divergence: kana outranks hangul, so the whole string must be scanned before deciding. Reading character by character and returning on the first hit answered Korean here.
same string, other order — the answer must not depend on which script comes first
Han + hangul and no kana: hangul settles it (the Han contributes nothing either way)
katakana phonetic extensions (U+31F0-31FF) count as kana
NFD-decomposed 가 is Hangul Jamo (U+1100-11FF), not a precomposed syllable
